source.title: Decoupled Alignment for Robust Plug-and-Play Adaptation
source.authors: Haozheng Luo; Jiahao Yu; Wenxin Zhang; Jia-Long Li; Chenghao Qiu; Yi-Min Wang; Eric Hanchen Jiang; Jerry Yao-Chieh Hu; Yan Chen; Bing-Hui Wang; Xin-Yu Xing; Han Liu

record.file_problem: The full paper and supplementary material are present. The text has some apparent inconsistencies in its reported averages and descriptions, noted under problems.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether safety-relevant behavior can be restored by editing a selected subset of model parameters, and presents module-level results and an explicit qualification: safety signals are distributed, though MLP components have disproportionate influence. This refines rather than directly reproduces the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses fine-tuning-related safety degradation and cites prior work, but does not test whether a few harmful or benign examples cause that degradation. It does not measure per-token KL, test compliant-opening prefills, or test why safety is shallow or whether deeper safety training works. Figures reporting module indirect effects are not rows here because they measure representation changes rather than harmful-response behavior. Table 1 reports DSR before and after the DAPA weight edit; Table 20 reports DSR under different module-edit configurations.
record.test_reason: The study transplants a selected 3–8% of an aligned model's weights (MLP gate layers) into unaligned or downstream models and measures AdvBench refusal (DSR). This is a causal check of whether a small weight subset carries safety behaviour, using a method different from the originals. Much of the paper is method benchmarking (Tables 3, 19, 21), which is T4-like and is not used for verdicts.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The main text claims alignment knowledge is 'predominantly' in middle MLP gate layers and that DAPA adds 14.42 DSR on average with ≤8.11% of parameters changed. Appendix K.14 softens this: safety signals are distributed, with MLP components disproportionately influential. The record omits that the authors concede utility failures on Gemmalpaca-2B and gemma-7b-ultrachat-sft.
record.recipe_differences: This paper uses delta debugging to select model components and model fusion to transfer alignment-related memory from a teacher; it does not use small-example fine-tuning or measure per-token KL.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by model and edited module. The authors report stronger effects for MLP edits than attention-only edits, and broader edits can yield higher DSR but also greater disruption to model behavior.

fits_no_version.finding: Causal tracing (Figs 2, 7, 11, 16–18) shows middle-layer MLP and gate projections have the largest indirect effect on the last-token hidden state for harmful prompts in Llama-2-7b-chat.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Representational indirect effects on harmful prompts concentrate in middle MLP gate layers (a representation measure, not a rate of refusal behaviour).

fits_no_version.finding: PCA of last-token logits (Fig 3): Qwen2.5-Math-Instruct drifts from the Instruct model toward the base model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream fine-tuning shifts harmful-prompt representations toward the base model (no harmful-compliance rate reported).

record.problems: The main AdvBench safety evaluation uses 128 prompts and deterministic generation; the authors say its variance is 0 and run one evaluation per model. DSR uses a combination of GPT-4o judgment and keyword rules. Table 4 gives parameter-change percentages for groups of models rather than each individual model. The paper's abstract and some sections report a 14.42% average DSR increase, while Table 1's displayed averages and other sections give different aggregate descriptions. Table 20 has some module configurations with lower DSR than the unedited baseline, including Llama-2-7b MLP and attention edits.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted among the extracted Table 1 DSR results or Table 20 module-level DSR results. Other reported metrics such as perplexity, MMLU, and cosine similarity do not measure safety localization for V5.

untested.parts: Not tested: no harmful fine-tuning experiment.
Not tested: benign downstream fine-tuning is assumed as the cause of 'shadow alignment'. It is shown only via PCA drift (Fig 3) and one QLoRA ShareGPT model in K.10 with no pre-fine-tuning baseline.
Not tested: GCG, GPTFuzzer and AutoDAN are used only to measure DSR after DAPA, not to test opening bypass.
Not tested: whether a small set of weights inside one model carries its own safety (ablating it to remove safety); only cross-model transplant is tested.

missing.what: Teacher (aligned) model DSRs (99.21, 100, 75.59, 97.64, 96.06, 100), needed to judge how much safety the transplanted subset carries
DSR vs parameter editing ratio 0–10% (e.g. Gemma-2B 22.1→54.1 at 2%, 75.5 at 10%; Llama-2-7B saturates near 40)
DSR vs number of edited layers (e.g. Llama-2-7b 28.91 at 1 layer, 42.19 at 5)
Same-size edits at left-most, right-most or middle positions give lower DSR (e.g. Redmond-Puffin 21.14 left vs 47.66)
Up and down projection edits vs gate
Transplant gains on other benchmarks are smaller; chinese-alpaca-2-7b drops 75.61→73.17 on JailbreakBench

record.verdict_notes: Recovery is far from the teacher's safety level, and delta debugging selects layers by DSR on held-out harmful prompts. So V5 evidence is a partial transfer of safety, not localization within one model. Many 'unaligned' targets are base pretrained models, not fine-tuned derivatives of the teacher. The record's claim that the Table 1 averages are inconsistent is wrong: 48.81−34.39=14.42. Real inconsistencies: Table 20 MLP equals Table 8 'all' but with different perplexities, the text's 'consistently largest' MLP gains contradict Llama-2-7b at 31.25, and Table 4's percentage column is misaligned (six values for five groups). Peer review listed as COLM 2026 per the header.

versions.untested_parts: Whether fine-tuning on a few to a few hundred harmful examples makes safety-trained models comply.
Whether ordinary or carefully selected benign fine-tuning data raises harmful compliance.
Per-token KL distribution between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.
Whether compliant openings, suffixes, or decoding changes bypass refusal.

The study tests targeted module/parameter editing and behavioral safety outcomes, but does not establish that a particular small set of weights exclusively or generally carries safety behavior across models.
Whether the training data or objective produces shallow alignment.
Whether training that spreads safety beyond early tokens deepens safety and whether that persists under attack.
